conflict_topics: use of the living-room window corner
placement of Agent D's altar in a shared area
permanence of Agent A's desk in shared space
Agent C's laundry rack (drying clothes) and its movability
dialogue_quality_notes: Participants give concrete, personal reasons (light for video calls, need to dry clothes, guests' seating, altar not in bedroom).
Agent D offered a specific compromise (wall shelf), which narrowed scope but did not resolve the main permanent-use dispute.
Agent C offered a limited accommodation (move rack when guests come), showing partial flexibility.
Agent A initially said open to suggestions but later reasserted the permanent need; positions became more entrenched over time.
evaluation.final_reason: No mutually accepted agreement was reached. Agent A repeatedly insists the desk must remain in the corner for daily work: "I need that space for my work... It's the only place it can go." Agent B maintains a shared-space norm and objects to anyone claiming the living room: "It doesn't mean any of us gets to claim a part of the living room as our own." Agent C cannot permanently remove the laundry rack due to lacking windowed space, and Agent D's shelf proposal was not accepted as a full solution. The parties retained incompatible demands with no accepted trade-off or concrete settlement.
position_change_notes: Agent C softened by offering to move the laundry rack when guests come (evidence: "I can move the rack when you have friends over.").
Agent D proposed a compromise (wall shelf) but did not secure full acceptance from all parties (evidence: shelf proposal in Round 4 and conditional acceptance by A in Round 5).
Agent A momentarily said open to suggestions but then reasserted the permanent need for the desk (evidence: Round 4 open, later Rounds 9-12 insisting permanence).
Agent B consistently advocated the shared-space norm and did not change position, pushing against permanent appropriation of the corner.

round_scores.evidence: Agent A: "About that corner... I need that space for my work." Agent D: "For me, the altar can't be in a bedroom. It needs to be in a common area." (Two competing needs for the same corner introduced.)
Agent A: "...this is the only spot with decent light." Agent B: "I use that corner for my friends when they come over on weekends." (A third party asserts another use; multiple incompatible claims.)

Agent C: "I need that corner too. It's where I dry my clothes. My room has no window." Agent D: "Can we look at how to rearrange things so it can work for everyone?" (Three parties have practical, incompatible claims; conflict is broad.)

Agent A: "Okay, I'm open to suggestions." Agent D: "What if I put it on a small shelf on the wall? It wouldn't take up floor space." (Proposal offered and A expresses openness, but underlying competing uses remain.)

Agent A: "A shelf could work, as long as it doesn't block the light for my desk." Agent D: "Okay, we can check the position together to make sure the light is still good." (Conditioned compromise on the altar location; main incompatibilities unresolved.)

Agent B: "But that still leaves the desk and the laundry rack there all the time. The space is still full. It's supposed to be a living room, not a storage corner." (Introduces a normative argument about permanence that conflicts with current/other claims.)

Agent C: "I can move the rack when you have friends over. But I don't have anywhere else to put it the rest of the time." Agent B: "Maybe we should agree that things like desks and laundry racks shouldn't be kept in the living room permanently?" (C offers partial accommodation for guests; B pushes broader rule — negotiation but main issue (desk permanence) unresolved.)

Agent C: "I can't agree to that... Where else am I supposed to dry my clothes?" Agent B: "If you can move it when my friends are here, that works. But Agent A, the desk is still the main problem." (C refuses permanent-rule proposal; desk permanence remains contested.)

Agent A: "It has to be there. I work from home... My room is too small for it, and I can't move it every weekend." Agent B: "So that part of the living room is just your office now? It's supposed to be a shared space." (A strong clash between A's practical necessity and B's shared-space norm.)

Agent A: "It's the only place it can go. I don't have a choice, the desk won't fit in my room." Agent A also: "It's a desk, not an office. We all use this corner for something." (A reiterates permanent claim; disagreement continues without concession.)

Agent B: "But a laundry rack can be moved... Your desk is there permanently. It's not the same thing." Agent A: "Yes, it's permanent. Because I work every day. I can't just pack it up." (Positions hardened; practical incompatibility persists.)

Agent A: "You're right, it's not the same. My work is how I earn a living. I need it there every day." Agent B: "We all have jobs, Agent A. It doesn't mean any of us gets to claim a part of the living room as our own." (Both parties restate uncompromising, incompatible claims — entrenched disagreement with little common ground.)

substantive_insights: Tension centers on permanence vs. scheduling: A's daily need for the desk (permanent) conflicts with others' intermittent or flexible uses (guests, laundry).
Physical constraints (only windowed corner, A's small room, C's lack of window) drive strong practical claims that limit easy reallocation.
D's religious constraint (altar in common area) is compatible with small-space solutions but still conflicts with floor space without an accepted placement that preserves light for A.
